title: The Woman Jericho Called a Prostitute—But God Wrote Her Into the Bloodline of Jesus
paragraphs: The Woman Jericho Called a Prostitute—But God Wrote Her Into the Bloodline of Jesus
How Rahab went from a condemned city and a scandalous past to the genealogy of Christ—and why her scarlet cord still whispers to every person who thinks their past has disqualified them from grace.
There is a woman in the genealogy of Jesus Christ whom many respectable people would probably have edited out.
Her name was Rahab.
And Scripture does not sanitize her story.

Before she became associated with Israel, before Hebrews remembered her for faith, before James pointed to the evidence of that faith, and centuries before Matthew placed her name in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ, Joshua introduced her with words that would have followed a woman like a scarlet letter:
רָחָב הַזּוֹנָה — Rāḥāḇ ha-zônāh.
Rahab the prostitute.
The Hebrew word זֹנָה (zônāh) refers to a prostitute. The New Testament remembers her similarly with the Greek expression Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute.”
God did not need the Bible to lie about Rahab's past in order to tell the truth about His grace.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to believe that one chapter has become our entire identity.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abandoned.
Promiscuous.
Angry.
Ashamed.
Lukewarm.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Maybe nobody else knows the word you secretly use for yourself.
But you do.
You remember what you did.
You remember who you were.

You remember the night you wish you could erase, the relationship you should never have entered, the compromise nobody discovered, the prayer you stopped praying, the promise you broke, the person you wounded, the years you wasted.
And sometimes the cruelest voice in the room is not another person's.
It is your own.
But Rahab's story forces us to confront a breathtaking truth:
God can tell the complete truth about your past without allowing your past to have the final word about your future.
Rahab lived in Jericho, a Canaanite city standing under divine judgment. When Joshua sent two men secretly to spy out the land, they entered Rahab's house.
Then something extraordinary happened.
Rahab hid them.
Why?
Not merely because she suddenly liked Israelites.
She had heard.

She told them that the inhabitants of the land had heard what the LORD had done—how He dried up the Red Sea and defeated Israel's enemies. Jericho had heard about Israel's God, and fear had fallen over the city.
But Rahab did something with what she heard.
She believed.
Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is astonishing:
“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
Behind the English word LORD stands God's covenant name in the Hebrew text:
יְהוָה — YHWH.
Rahab was confessing the supremacy of Israel's God while living inside a culture destined for judgment.
Think about that.
She had no respectable Israelite pedigree.
No childhood memories of Moses.
No wilderness testimony.
No ancestry descending from Abraham.
She was a Canaanite.
A woman.
A prostitute.
A resident of Jericho.
From a human perspective, she appeared to be standing on the wrong side of almost every boundary.
Yet faith crossed the boundary.
That does not mean Rahab earned salvation by becoming morally impressive overnight. Scripture refuses to turn her story into salvation by human merit.
Hebrews 11:31 places the emphasis exactly where it belongs:
“By faith…”
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη… — Pistei Rhaab hē pornē…
“By faith, Rahab the prostitute…”
That first word matters.
Πίστει — pistei — “by faith.”
Rahab's actions mattered because they revealed that her confession was more than frightened religious language.
She trusted the God she confessed.

James later points to Rahab when explaining that genuine faith does not remain sterile and invisible. She received the messengers and sent them out another way. Her works did not function as a price with which she purchased God's grace; they demonstrated the reality of a faith that acted. James explicitly remembers what she did.
This distinction matters enormously.
Christianity does not teach, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps God will finally love you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
God saves sinners by grace through faith, and the faith that truly encounters Him begins producing a changed life.
Rahab believed.
And because she believed, she acted.
There comes a moment when faith stops being something you merely say and becomes something you stake your life upon.
Rahab reached that moment.
Imagine the scene.
Jericho's authorities are searching.
Two Israelite spies are hidden.
Rahab knows discovery could cost her everything.
She has to choose.
The city she can see…
or the God she has only heard about.
The old allegiance…
or a terrifying new faith.
Safety as she understood it…
or surrender to the God of Israel.
And somewhere in that decision, Rahab crossed an invisible line.
Her address was still Jericho.
Her history was still real.
Her past had not magically disappeared.
But her allegiance had changed.
That may be the word someone reading this needs.
Repentance is not pretending yesterday never happened.
It is turning toward God today.
The Gospel does not require you to manufacture a cleaner history before coming to Jesus.
It calls you to come to Jesus with the history you actually have.
Rahab then pleaded for mercy not only for herself but for her family.
The spies agreed. A scarlet cord was to hang from her window, identifying the house whose occupants would be spared when judgment came upon Jericho.
A scarlet cord.
It is difficult for a Christian reader not to feel the theological resonance.
But we should be careful here.
Scripture itself does not explicitly say that Rahab's scarlet cord was a prophecy of the blood of Christ. We should not claim more than the Bible claims.

Yet within the Bible's larger story, the imagery can certainly remind Christians of a greater rescue: judgment is real, refuge is necessary, and ultimately sinners are saved not by their moral record but through God's provision, fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ and His atoning death.
Rahab's cord was not Jesus' blood.
But Rahab's rescue belongs to the same unfolding biblical story that eventually leads us to the cross.
And when Jericho fell, Rahab lived.
Hebrews remembers the reason: “By faith.” She did not perish with the disobedient because she welcomed the spies in peace.
But surviving Jericho was not the most astonishing thing God would do with Rahab's story.
Because generations later, Matthew opens his Gospel.
And genealogies begin.
Names.
Fathers.
Sons.
Generations.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Then suddenly…
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 identifies Salmon as the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz becomes the father of Obed, Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David.
Follow that line forward through the generations and Matthew brings us to Jesus Christ.
Do you understand what that means?
The woman once identified with Jericho's prostitution became part of the family line through which the Messiah entered history.
Rahab was connected to Jesus through the genealogy Matthew records.
She was an ancestor in the Messianic line.
The scandal was not erased from Scripture.
Grace simply wrote beyond it.
And this is where Rahab stops being merely an ancient character and begins standing uncomfortably close to us.
Because perhaps you have secretly assumed that Jesus wants people with cleaner biographies.
People who did not sleep with that person.
People who did not destroy that marriage.
People who did not waste those years.
People who did not relapse.
People who did not walk away from church.
People who do not carry your memories.
You look at Christians whose lives appear polished and think, Maybe God can use them.
Then you look at yourself and think, But He knows me.
Yes.
He does.
That is precisely what makes grace grace.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed minor improvement.
He came because sinners needed rescue.
The cross destroys both despair and pride.
It destroys despair because no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
And it destroys pride because nobody enters God's kingdom because his résumé was impressive enough.
At Calvary, respectable sinners and publicly scandalous sinners have the same need.
Mercy.
This does not mean sin is insignificant.
Grace never required God to rename evil as good.
Jesus' mercy is precious precisely because sin is serious.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says something far more costly:
Your sin mattered enough that Christ went to the cross, and His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to remain your master.
That is the difference between cheap reassurance and biblical redemption.
Jesus does not merely improve reputations.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He transforms.
And He gives sinners a new identity in Himself.
Maybe you have spent years trying to hide your Jericho.
Rahab's story says you can stop pretending.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Not because Rahab saved herself.
Not because you can save yourself.
But because the Savior who eventually came through Rahab's family line came specifically to save sinners.
That baby Matthew introduces after recording generations of complicated human history eventually walked toward a Roman cross.
There He carried sin.
There He endured judgment.
There He shed His blood.
There He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is why your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Not because positive thinking can rewrite you.
Not because religion can rewrite you.
Not because a motivational article can rewrite you.
Because Jesus Christ can.
Rahab was once part of a condemned city.
Then she became part of God's people.
Her story appeared among the heroes of faith.
Her actions became an apostolic illustration of living faith.
And her name appeared in the genealogy leading to Christ.
The Bible remembered what she had been.
But heaven's story revealed what grace could do.
That is from scandal to grace.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is that Rahab's story never becomes mainly about Rahab.
It points beyond her.
Toward Jesus.
Every redeemed sinner's testimony eventually must.
Maybe your testimony begins with addiction.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe sexual sin.
Maybe pride.
Maybe religion without Christ.
Maybe years of pretending.
Maybe nobody would call your history scandalous, but you know how far your heart has wandered from God.
Whatever the beginning, redemption has one center:
Jesus Christ.
So do not turn Rahab into permission to remain where sin left you.
Rahab did not stay aligned with Jericho.
Faith changed her allegiance.
Grace calls us out.
Jesus receives sinners, but He does not call us to make peace with the chains from which He came to free us.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
And if you have already trusted Christ but shame keeps dragging old photographs from your past into your mind, remember Rahab.
God was not embarrassed to put her name in Matthew 1.
Perhaps you are still introducing yourself by a name Christ died to free you from.
“Dirty.”
“Ruined.”
“Unworthy.”
“Too far gone.”
But for everyone who is truly in Christ, Scripture gives language stronger than shame: forgiven, reconciled, redeemed, adopted, made new.
Your scars may remain part of your testimony.
They do not have to remain your identity.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list needs to hear this tonight.
Not eventually.
Now.
Someone is smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God could possibly want them after what they have done.
Your comment may become the courage someone else needs to stop pretending.

Gospel Warrior exists because biblical truth should not merely fill a feed. It should reach wounded people, confront sin, announce grace, strengthen disciples, and keep pointing hearts back to Jesus Christ.

We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, worship, love, generosity, and faithful witness. But when you freely support Gospel work that genuinely serves Christ, that support can help biblical encouragement reach people who desperately need it.
Not because a share saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sharing can put the message of Jesus in front of someone you may never realize was quietly searching for hope.
Invite your family.
Send it to the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Let the seeker read it.
Let the lukewarm Christian wrestle with it.
Let the person drowning in shame discover Rahab standing in Matthew's genealogy.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody believes their scandal is stronger than God's grace.
Rahab's name says otherwise.
The cross says otherwise.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain nights still hurt.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Christ does.
Jericho knew Rahab by her scandal; Scripture remembers her by faith—and generations later, her name stood in the earthly family line leading to Jesus.
